newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia lending rates seen higher before easing.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia lending rates seen higher before easing.

text.p: Malaysian bank base lending rates are expected to inch up further before easing towards the end of the year, economists said on Tuesday.
Higher average interbank rates this month could lead to another round of increases in the BLR -- the benchmark commercial loan rate banks offer to their best clients -- in July, they said.
"We may see another 15 basis point increase in July before rates start to fall back," said Sani Hamid, an analyst at research house MMS International in Singapore.
Banks had raised their BLR by an average 30 basis points after interbank rates surged in May due to a sudden tightening of liquidity in the banking system.
The draining of funds was caused by a massive intervention by Bank Negara which joined other central banks to fight off a speculative attack on regional currencies.

Money market dealers said the central bank intervention mopped up around four billion ringgit ($1.6 billion) from the system. It pushed overnight interbank rates to above 20 percent while one- and three-month money jumped to over nine percent from around 7.3 percent.
Under a new formula announced in October 1995, the BLR is pegged to the average three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate over a month.
The central bank then fixes a ceiling rate.
The ceiling in May was fixed at 9.62 percent, and most banks, with the exception of Malaysia's top bank Malayan Banking, are now quoting BLRs at 9.60 percent.
Bank Negara said then that the situation was temporary.
Economists expect banks to raise their BLR close to the maximum level allowed due to the rise in interbank rates.
Although interbank rates have come down, with three-month money currently quoted at 7.60/70 percent, they are still higher than before May.
Sani said he expected Malayan Banking (Maybank) also to start raising its BLR soon. "To reflect the cost of funding, the bank will have to raise its BLR," he said.
Maybank managing director Amirsham Abdul Aziz said last week that the bank may raise its BLR if interbank rates do not ease from a recent spike. Maybank's BLR is at 9.10 percent.
But economists noted that a climate of higher interest rates may not last long.
"Our view is for rates to ease by 30 to 50 basis points in the second half of the year," said Rajeev Malik, an economist at Singapore-based Jardine Fleming Research.
He cited slower loan growth as among the key factors which would lead to lower rates.
Loans growth slowed to 28.5 percent year-on-year in April against 29.6 percent in March as curbs on bank loans for property and stock purchases began to take effect.

Bank Negara announced on March 28 it was requiring banks and finance companies to trim exposure to the property sector to 20 percent of total outstanding loans. New restrictions were also placed on financing stock purchases.
The central bank said it was taking "pre-emptive action" to prevent a speculative bubble forming in the economy.
Malik expects loans growth to slow to 18 percent by the end of the year.
Capitalcorp Securities economist Zulkifli Hamzah said the chance of interest rates going higher was slim.
"At most, they will be flat. But there's room for rates to come off later in the year," he said. ($1 = 2.51 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
